result.summary: Euphaes drills the Messenians and both sides raid each other's lands. In a first battle across a ravine, Euphaes' fortified camp makes the Lacedæmonians give up and go home. A year later two Spartan kings lead a second campaign, and the commanders exhort their armies before the battle.

scenes.title: Training and raiding
scenes.summary: Euphaes keeps the Messenians armed and trained. The Lacedæmonians raid Messenia without taking any towns, while the Messenians plunder Laconia.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk losing their land and towns to Spartan raids.

scenes.title: Battle at the ravine
scenes.summary: Euphaes marches out and draws up his army behind a ravine. His slaves fortify the camp while the cavalry fight, and the Lacedæmonians give up and go home.
scenes.stakes: Defeat in open battle could end Messenian resistance.

place.name: A place in Messenia with a ravine

scenes.title: Second campaign and speeches
scenes.summary: Both Spartan kings lead a second campaign and the armies form up. Theopompus and Euphaes exhort their men, Euphaes warning of the horrors of defeat.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians face slavery, death and destruction of their country if defeated.

notable_quotes.reason: Shows Euphaes' tactical cunning in fortifying the camp so the Spartans cannot fight.

analysis.text: Careful preparation and strategy let the weaker Messenians hold off Sparta.
Speeches before battle are a standard device of Greek historiography, here placed in the mouths of leaders of the early Messenian War.

language_notes.text: The Spartans spared trees and houses because they claimed Messenia as their own future possession, and took only movable goods such as livestock and crops.
"Dawned upon" means became clear to them; the army's cleverness was realized the next morning.
Siege train: the heavy equipment and engines needed to assault a fortified position.
"The old man" is Euphaes' taunting of the Spartans; the phrase appears to refer to him, though he is a king, and is loosely used.
"For the nonce" means for the occasion; Euryleon was a Theban by origin but was serving Sparta at that time.
Harangue: a forceful speech meant to rouse an audience.

context_notes.text: Mount Taygetus is the mountain range west of Sparta, separating Laconia from Messenia.
Sparta had two hereditary kings at once, who commonly led the army together.
Amphea was a Messenian town seized by Sparta at the start of the war, and its captives were mistreated.

literary_notes.text: Messenians "boiling over with rage" compares anger to a liquid heated until it spills, conveying their eagerness for war.
Euphaes' skill "dawned upon" the Spartans like daylight, giving the realization a sense of gradual, inescapable revelation.
Euphaes builds a list of escalating horrors, captives, death, outrage, plunder, fire, to make defeat feel unbearable and spur courage.
